items.stem: What is the symbol for a cell?
options: A long thin line and a short thick line
items.answer: A long thin line and a short thick line
items.markingKey: B. The long line is positive.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a series circuit and a parallel circuit.
items.answer: A series circuit has one path, so components share the pd and one break stops everything; a parallel circuit has separate branches, each with the full pd, so components work independently.
items.markingKey: A series circuit has one path, so components share the pd and one break stops everything; a parallel circuit has separate branches, each with the full pd, so components work independently. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Current is used up by each lamp in a series circuit." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit; energy, not current, is transferred to the lamps.
items.markingKey: Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit; energy, not current, is transferred to the lamps. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Mohammed measured the current from a 6 V supply when different numbers of identical lamps were connected in parallel.

Number of lamps | Total current / A: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 0.26 | 0.27 | 0.25
2 | 0.53 | 0.51 | 0.53
3 | 0.74 | 0.79 | 0.77
4 | 1.04 | 0.98 | 1.05
5 | 1.25 | 1.23 | 1.23

Calculate the mean total current when the number of lamps was 3.
items.markingKey: M1 (0.74 + 0.79 + 0.77) ÷ 3; A1 0.77 A (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of lamps in series affects the brightness of each lamp, state the dependent variable and describe how Kwame should measure it.
items.answer: brightness of one lamp measured with a light meter (lux) at 10 cm
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: brightness of one lamp measured with a light meter (lux) at 10 cm.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Learning circuits with simulation software is as good as building real circuits."
items.answer: Simulations are useful for understanding, but students also need hands-on practice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: safe, quick, no broken components; shows current and pd values clearly. Arguments against: no practice handling real equipment or finding loose connections; real components behave less ideally. Supported judgement: Simulations are useful for understanding, but students also need hands-on practice.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "series circuit"?
options: A resistor whose resistance can be changed to control the current
A circuit with only one path for the current
A property of particles such as electrons; flowing charge forms a current
items.answer: A circuit with only one path for the current
items.markingKey: B. "series circuit" is a circuit with only one path for the current.

items.stem: Briefly explain why lamps in parallel stay bright when more lamps are added.
items.answer: Each branch receives the full potential difference of the supply, so each lamp has the same pd and current as if it were alone.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each branch receives the full potential difference of the supply, so each lamp has the same pd and current as if it were alone. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: 3 cells, each 1.5 V, are connected in series to 3 identical lamps in series. Calculate the total pd of the battery and the pd across each lamp.
items.answer: 4.5 V; 1.5 V each
items.markingKey: M1 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V; M1 shared equally between 3 lamps; A1 1.5 V.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of lamps in series affects the brightness of each lamp. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Connect one lamp to a 6 V supply; measure the light intensity 10 cm from it with a light meter; add a second identical lamp in series and remeasure the first lamp; continue to four lamps; repeat three times; also measure current with an ammeter.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (lamps get hot – do not touch; switch off between readings; use low-voltage supplies only). Model: Connect one lamp to a 6 V supply; measure the light intensity 10 cm from it with a light meter; add a second identical lamp in series and remeasure the first lamp; continue to four lamps; repeat three times; also measure current with an ammeter.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V)"?
items.answer: potential difference (voltage)
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of potential difference (voltage).

items.stem: Explain the difference between an ammeter and a voltmeter.
items.answer: An ammeter measures current, is connected in series and has very low resistance; a voltmeter measures pd, is connected in parallel and has very high resistance.
items.markingKey: An ammeter measures current, is connected in series and has very low resistance; a voltmeter measures pd, is connected in parallel and has very high resistance. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why an ammeter must have a very low resistance.
items.answer: It is placed in series, so a high resistance would reduce the current it is trying to measure.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is placed in series, so a high resistance would reduce the current it is trying to measure. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Current gets used up as it goes round the circuit." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Current is the same before and after a component in series; energy is transferred, not charge.
items.markingKey: Current is the same before and after a component in series; energy is transferred, not charge. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a parallel circuit the branch currents are 1.2 A, 0.8 A and 0.1 A. What current flows from the supply?
items.markingKey: M1 currents in parallel branches add: 1.2 + 0.8 + 0.1; A1 2.1 A.

items.stem:
Kenji measured the current through a fixed resistor for different potential differences across it.

Potential difference / V | Current / A: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1.0 | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.10
2.0 | 0.19 | 0.19 | 0.20
3.0 | 0.28 | 0.30 | 0.28
4.0 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.38
5.0 | 0.47 | 0.47 | 0.49

State the potential difference at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 5.0 V; range = 0.02 A; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 5.0 V; 1 range = max − min = 0.49 − 0.47 = 0.02 A; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: In a parallel circuit, a 6 V battery supplies two branches: branch A has one lamp, branch B has two identical lamps in series. Predict the pd across each lamp and compare the currents, explaining your reasoning.
items.answer: Each branch has the full 6 V; lamp in A: 6 V; each lamp in B: 3 V (shared in series). Branch B has twice the resistance so half the current of branch A; total current from the battery = sum of branch currents; lamps in B are dimmer.
items.markingKey: Each branch has the full 6 V; lamp in A: 6 V; each lamp in B: 3 V (shared in series). Branch B has twice the resistance so half the current of branch A; total current from the battery = sum of branch currents; lamps in B are dimmer.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of cells in series affects the current through a lamp. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Build a circuit with one cell, a switch, an ammeter in series and a lamp; connect a voltmeter across the lamp; close the switch and record current and pd; add cells one at a time; repeat three times; plot current against pd.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (do not exceed the lamp’s rated voltage; lamps get hot). Model: Build a circuit with one cell, a switch, an ammeter in series and a lamp; connect a voltmeter across the lamp; close the switch and record current and pd; add cells one at a time; repeat three times; plot current against pd.

items.stem: Define the term "charge".
items.answer: A property of particles such as electrons; flowing charge forms a current
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a property of particles such as electrons; flowing charge forms a current. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between current and potential difference.
items.answer: Current is the rate of flow of charge through a component (A, measured in series); potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points (V, measured in parallel).
items.markingKey: Current is the rate of flow of charge through a component (A, measured in series); potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points (V, measured in parallel). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Alessandro Volta’s pile (1800) shows source of potential difference.
items.answer: Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cloth soaked in salt water, making the first battery that produced a steady current. The volt is named after him, and his battery made the study of electric currents possible.
items.markingKey: Context (Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cloth soaked in salt water, making the first battery that produced a steady current.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The volt is named after him, and his battery made the study of electric currents possible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to source of potential difference.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The water-in-pipes model is a good way to explain current and potential difference."
items.answer: Models such as water pipes help at first, but their limitations should be discussed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: current like flow rate of water, pd like pressure difference – easy to picture. Arguments against: water can leak from pipes, but charge does not leave wires; misleading for parallel circuits and for what pd really is. Supported judgement: Models such as water pipes help at first, but their limitations should be discussed. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: What happens to the resistance of a wire as it gets longer?
items.answer: It increases
items.markingKey: C. Electrons collide with more ions.

items.stem: Briefly explain why thicker wires are used for high-current appliances such as cookers.
items.answer: Thicker wires have lower resistance, so less energy is wasted as heat and the wire does not overheat.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Thicker wires have lower resistance, so less energy is wasted as heat and the wire does not overheat. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "All components obey Ohm’s law." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only ohmic conductors such as fixed resistors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not.
items.markingKey: Only ohmic conductors such as fixed resistors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A pd of 50 V across a resistor produces a current of 0.5 A. Calculate its resistance.
Lukas plans to investigate how the length of a constantan wire affects its resistance. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: diameter of the wire; material (constantan); temperature (low current, switch off between readings); the same meters
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: diameter of the wire – thicker wire has lower resistance; material (constantan) – materials differ in resistivity; temperature (low current, switch off between readings) – heating increases resistance; the same meters – calibration differences. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Amara measured the resistance of a thermistor at different temperatures in a water bath (three readings each).

Temperature / °C | Resistance / Ω: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 1179 | 1197 | 1200
20 | 823 | 832 | 802
30 | 531 | 565 | 562
40 | 368 | 377 | 362
50 | 254 | 239 | 253

Calculate the mean resistance when the temperature was 50 °C.
items.markingKey: M1 (254 + 239 + 253) ÷ 3; A1 248.7 Ω (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Describe how to investigate how the length of a wire affects its resistance, including the circuit, measurements, calculation and how to make it a fair test.
items.answer: Circuit: cell, ammeter in series with a length of constantan wire on a metre rule (crocodile clips), voltmeter across the wire. Vary length 10–100 cm; record I and V; R = V ÷ I; repeat; keep the same wire (material, thickness), low current and switch off between readings so temperature stays constant; plot R against length – expect straight line through origin.
items.markingKey: Circuit: cell, ammeter in series with a length of constantan wire on a metre rule (crocodile clips), voltmeter across the wire. Vary length 10–100 cm; record I and V; R = V ÷ I; repeat; keep the same wire (material, thickness), low current and switch off between readings so temperature stays constant; plot R against length – expect straight line through origin.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the length of a constantan wire affects its resistance. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Tape the wire along a metre rule; connect a cell, switch and ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the wire; set the clips 20 cm apart; close the switch briefly and record I and V; repeat for each length; repeat three times; calculate R and plot against length.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (the wire can get hot – keep currents low and do not touch it while current flows). Model: Tape the wire along a metre rule; connect a cell, switch and ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the wire; set the clips 20 cm apart; close the switch briefly and record I and V; repeat for each length; repeat three times; calculate R and plot against length.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a dimmer switch can control the brightness of a lamp.
items.answer: It is a variable resistor; increasing its resistance decreases the current, so the lamp is dimmer.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is a variable resistor; increasing its resistance decreases the current, so the lamp is dimmer. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an LDR and a thermistor.
items.answer: A thermistor’s resistance falls as temperature rises; an LDR’s resistance falls as light intensity increases.
items.markingKey: A thermistor’s resistance falls as temperature rises; an LDR’s resistance falls as light intensity increases. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Superconductors and MRI scanners as an example, explain resistance in technology.
items.answer: Some materials lose all resistance when cooled below a critical temperature; MRI scanners use superconducting coils cooled by liquid helium to make strong magnetic fields. Zero resistance means huge currents with no heating, but cooling is expensive.
items.markingKey: Context (Some materials lose all resistance when cooled below a critical temperature; MRI scanners use superconducting coils cooled by liquid helium to make strong magnetic fields.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Zero resistance means huge currents with no heating, but cooling is expensive. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resistance in technology.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Research into room-temperature superconductors should be a top priority for funding."
items.answer: It is worth funding as long-term research, but alongside proven energy solutions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: would remove energy losses in power lines; cheaper MRI, faster computers, maglev trains. Arguments against: may never be achieved; many claims have been false; money could go to proven technologies like renewables. Supported judgement: It is worth funding as long-term research, but alongside proven energy solutions. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "earth wire".
items.answer: The green-and-yellow wire that carries current safely to earth if a metal case becomes live
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the green-and-yellow wire that carries current safely to earth if a metal case becomes live. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "A higher-power appliance always costs more to run." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cost depends on power and how long it is used; a 2 kW kettle used for 3 minutes costs less than a 100 W TV used all evening.
items.markingKey: Cost depends on power and how long it is used; a 2 kW kettle used for 3 minutes costs less than a 100 W TV used all evening. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a circuit breaker and a fuse.
items.answer: A fuse is a thin wire that melts and must be replaced; a circuit breaker is an automatic switch that trips faster and can be reset.
items.markingKey: A fuse is a thin wire that melts and must be replaced; a circuit breaker is an automatic switch that trips faster and can be reset. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Elena used a plug-in energy monitor to measure the energy used by a fan heater running for different times.

Time / h | Energy used / kWh: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.5 | 0.88 | 0.84 | 0.84
1.0 | 1.74 | 1.78 | 1.76
1.5 | 2.56 | 2.62 | 2.68
2.0 | 3.51 | 3.56 | 3.60
2.5 | 4.42 | 4.38 | 4.27

Calculate the mean energy used when the time was 0.5 h.
items.answer: 0.85 kWh
items.markingKey: M1 (0.88 + 0.84 + 0.84) ÷ 3; A1 0.85 kWh (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: A 2.4 kW kettle is used for 1.5 hours. Electricity costs 20p per kWh. Calculate the cost.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Smart meters help households save energy."
items.answer: Smart meters can help, but savings depend on people changing their habits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: show real-time energy use and cost, encouraging changes; accurate bills without estimates. Arguments against: savings are often small once novelty wears off; privacy concerns about usage data. Supported judgement: Smart meters can help, but savings depend on people changing their habits.

items.stem: What is the power of a kettle using 230 V and 10 A?
items.markingKey: A. P = V × I.

items.stem: Briefly explain why electricity bills use kWh rather than joules.
items.answer: Joules are tiny; a typical home uses billions of joules a month, so kWh gives manageable numbers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Joules are tiny; a typical home uses billions of joules a month, so kWh gives manageable numbers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Residual current devices (RCDs) and explain what it reveals about electrical safety.
items.answer: RCDs compare current in live and neutral wires and switch off within about 30 ms if there is a difference, such as current leaking through a person. Required in new homes in many countries, they prevent many electrocutions, especially with outdoor equipment.
items.markingKey: Context (RCDs compare current in live and neutral wires and switch off within about 30 ms if there is a difference, such as current leaking through a person.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Required in new homes in many countries, they prevent many electrocutions, especially with outdoor equipment. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electrical safety.

items.stem: Define the term "electromagnet".
items.answer: A coil of wire, usually around an iron core, that becomes magnetic when current flows
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a coil of wire, usually around an iron core, that becomes magnetic when current flows. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Rubbing gives objects positive charge by adding protons." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction; losing electrons leaves an object positive.
items.markingKey: Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction; losing electrons leaves an object positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the current in an electromagnet affects the number of paper clips it can hold, state the dependent variable and describe how Mohammed should measure it.
items.answer: number of paper clips picked up
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: number of paper clips picked up.

items.stem:
Mei measured the force between two magnets at different separations using a balance (three readings each).

Separation / cm | Force / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 2.71 | 2.64 | 2.66
2 | 0.67 | 0.66 | 0.68
3 | 0.29 | 0.31 | 0.30
4 | 0.17 | 0.16 | 0.17
5 | 0.11 | 0.11 | 0.11

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The force decreases rapidly as the separation increases – doubling the distance reduces the force to about a quarter. The magnetic field gets weaker with distance from the magnets, so the force between them falls sharply.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The force decreases rapidly as the separation increases – doubling the distance reduces the force to about a quarter.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: The magnetic field gets weaker with distance from the magnets, so the force between them falls sharply.

items.stem: Tariq plans an investigation into how the current in an electromagnet affects the number of paper clips it can hold. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (current through the coil (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 A)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Explain why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.
items.answer: The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface slightly positive, so the balloon is attracted.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The negative balloon repels electrons in the wall surface away, leaving the surface slightly positive, so the balloon is attracted. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Maglev trains, explain how it illustrates magnetism in transport.
items.answer: Maglev trains in Shanghai and Japan use powerful electromagnets to lift the train above the track and push it forward, reaching over 400 km/h. No wheel friction allows very high speeds, but the tracks are very expensive to build.
items.markingKey: Context (Maglev trains in Shanghai and Japan use powerful electromagnets to lift the train above the track and push it forward, reaching over 400 km/h.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: No wheel friction allows very high speeds, but the tracks are very expensive to build. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to magnetism in transport.

items.stem: In a parallel circuit, the currents in two branches are 0.3 A and 0.5 A. What is the current from the cell?
items.markingKey: C. Branch currents add.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A resistor whose resistance decreases as temperature increases"?
items.answer: thermistor
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of thermistor.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "series circuit".
items.answer: A circuit with only one path for the current
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a circuit with only one path for the current. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between energy and power.
items.answer: Power is the rate of transfer (W); energy is the total transferred (J or kWh) = power × time.
items.markingKey: Power is the rate of transfer (W); energy is the total transferred (J or kWh) = power × time. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between an electromagnet and a permanent magnet.
items.answer: A permanent magnet is always magnetic and has a fixed strength; an electromagnet is only magnetic when current flows and its strength can be changed.
items.markingKey: A permanent magnet is always magnetic and has a fixed strength; an electromagnet is only magnetic when current flows and its strength can be changed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit.
items.answer: There is only one path, and charge is not used up, so the same amount of charge passes every point each second.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There is only one path, and charge is not used up, so the same amount of charge passes every point each second. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a fixed resistor and a filament lamp.
items.answer: A fixed resistor has constant resistance at constant temperature, giving a straight-line I–V graph; a filament lamp’s resistance increases as it heats up, giving a curved graph.
items.markingKey: A fixed resistor has constant resistance at constant temperature, giving a straight-line I–V graph; a filament lamp’s resistance increases as it heats up, giving a curved graph. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Adding more cells in parallel makes lamps brighter." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Identical cells in parallel give the same pd as one cell; they just last longer. Cells in series increase the pd.
items.markingKey: Identical cells in parallel give the same pd as one cell; they just last longer. Cells in series increase the pd. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "The neutral wire is always completely safe to touch." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Faults can make the neutral wire carry a dangerous pd; never touch any wires in a live circuit.
items.markingKey: Faults can make the neutral wire carry a dangerous pd; never touch any wires in a live circuit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.markingKey: Only ohmic conductors such as fixed resistors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars wants to find out how the number of lamps in series affects the brightness of each lamp. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.

items.stem: Rafael wants to find out how the power rating of an electric kettle affects the time it takes to boil 1 litre of water. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does power rating of the kettle affect time for 1 dm³ of water to reach boiling?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (power rating of the kettle (1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 kW)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (time for 1 dm³ of water to reach boiling (switch-off)) in a question form.

items.stem: Briefly describe Maglev trains and explain what it reveals about magnetism in transport.
items.answer: Maglev trains in Shanghai and Japan use powerful electromagnets to lift the train above the track and push it forward, reaching over 400 km/h. No wheel friction allows very high speeds, but the tracks are very expensive to build.
items.markingKey: Context (Maglev trains in Shanghai and Japan use powerful electromagnets to lift the train above the track and push it forward, reaching over 400 km/h.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: No wheel friction allows very high speeds, but the tracks are very expensive to build. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to magnetism in transport.

items.stem:
Isabel measured the current through a fixed resistor for different potential differences across it.

Potential difference / V | Current / A: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1.0 | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.09
2.0 | 0.19 | 0.19 | 0.19
3.0 | 0.29 | 0.28 | 0.29
4.0 | 0.39 | 0.38 | 0.39
5.0 | 0.48 | 0.49 | 0.47

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The current increases in direct proportion to the potential difference. At constant temperature a resistor has a constant resistance (Ohm’s law), so I = V ÷ R gives a straight line through the origin.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The current increases in direct proportion to the potential difference.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At constant temperature a resistor has a constant resistance (Ohm’s law), so I = V ÷ R gives a straight line through the origin.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Research into room-temperature superconductors should be a top priority for funding."
items.answer: It is worth funding as long-term research, but alongside proven energy solutions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: would remove energy losses in power lines; cheaper MRI, faster computers, maglev trains. Arguments against: may never be achieved; many claims have been false; money could go to proven technologies like renewables. Supported judgement: It is worth funding as long-term research, but alongside proven energy solutions.

items.stem: Design a circuit for a model house with two rooms, where each room has a lamp with its own switch, and a main switch that turns everything off. Describe (draw) the circuit and explain your choices.
items.answer: Main switch in series with the cell, before the branches; two parallel branches, each with a lamp and its own switch in series. Parallel: each lamp gets full pd (bright) and can be switched independently; the main switch in the main line breaks the whole circuit. A fuse in the main line adds safety.
items.markingKey: Main switch in series with the cell, before the branches; two parallel branches, each with a lamp and its own switch in series. Parallel: each lamp gets full pd (bright) and can be switched independently; the main switch in the main line breaks the whole circuit. A fuse in the main line adds safety.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the power rating of an electric kettle affects the time it takes to boil 1 litre of water. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): steam and boiling water scald – keep away from the spout; dry hands near mains sockets. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. steam and boiling water scald – keep away from the spout; dry hands near mains sockets); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Maglev trains should replace high-speed rail." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Maglev suits some busy routes between big cities, but conventional high-speed rail is usually more practical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: faster, quieter, less wear and maintenance; no wheel friction. Arguments against: very expensive dedicated tracks; cannot use existing railway network. Supported judgement: Maglev suits some busy routes between big cities, but conventional high-speed rail is usually more practical. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "current"?
options: The current through a resistor at constant temperature is directly proportional to the potential difference across it (V = I × R)
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A)
A circuit with only one path for the current
items.answer: The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A)
items.markingKey: B. "current" is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).

items.stem: Define the term "variable resistor".
items.answer: A resistor whose resistance can be changed to control the current
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a resistor whose resistance can be changed to control the current. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A single source of potential difference; a battery is two or more cells"?
items.answer: cell
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of cell.

items.stem: Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect a person if a live wire touches a metal kettle case.
items.answer: A large current flows from the live wire through the case to earth; this melts the fuse, disconnecting the live wire, so the case is no longer dangerous.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A large current flows from the live wire through the case to earth; this melts the fuse, disconnecting the live wire, so the case is no longer dangerous. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why you sometimes get a small electric shock from a car door after a journey.
items.answer: Friction between your clothes and the seat transfers electrons, charging you; when you touch the metal door the charge flows suddenly through you to earth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Friction between your clothes and the seat transfers electrons, charging you; when you touch the metal door the charge flows suddenly through you to earth. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Voltage flows through a circuit." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Potential difference is between two points; it is current (charge) that flows.
items.markingKey: Potential difference is between two points; it is current (charge) that flows. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Resistance is the same as current." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Resistance opposes current; for a given pd, higher resistance means lower current.
items.markingKey: Resistance opposes current; for a given pd, higher resistance means lower current. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Christmas tree lights in series all go out if one bulb fails.
items.answer: There is only one path; a broken filament breaks the circuit, so no current flows through any bulb.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There is only one path; a broken filament breaks the circuit, so no current flows through any bulb. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the fuse rating should be just above the normal current of the appliance.
items.answer: It must not blow in normal use, but must melt quickly if a fault causes a larger current.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It must not blow in normal use, but must melt quickly if a fault causes a larger current. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tomás wants to find out how the current in an electromagnet affects the number of paper clips it can hold. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does current through the coil affect number of paper clips picked up?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (current through the coil (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 A)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (number of paper clips picked up) in a question form.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of cells in series affects the current through a lamp, state the dependent variable and describe how Mohammed should measure it.
items.answer: current through the lamp measured with an ammeter in series
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: current through the lamp measured with an ammeter in series.

items.stem: A current of 0.1 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. Calculate the pd across it.
items.answer: 2 V

items.stem:
Ana measured the current from a 6 V supply when different numbers of identical lamps were connected in parallel.

Number of lamps | Total current / A: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 0.28 | 0.27 | 0.27
2 | 0.55 | 0.54 | 0.52
3 | 0.83 | 0.81 | 0.80
4 | 1.10 | 1.09 | 1.11
5 | 1.34 | 1.38 | 1.32

Calculate the mean total current when the number of lamps was 1.
items.markingKey: M1 (0.28 + 0.27 + 0.27) ÷ 3; A1 0.27 A (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Residual current devices (RCDs) shows electrical safety.
items.answer: RCDs compare current in live and neutral wires and switch off within about 30 ms if there is a difference, such as current leaking through a person. Required in new homes in many countries, they prevent many electrocutions, especially with outdoor equipment.
items.markingKey: Context (RCDs compare current in live and neutral wires and switch off within about 30 ms if there is a difference, such as current leaking through a person.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Required in new homes in many countries, they prevent many electrocutions, especially with outdoor equipment. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electrical safety.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Rubbing gives objects positive charge by adding protons." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction; losing electrons leaves an object positive.
items.markingKey: Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction; losing electrons leaves an object positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Alessandro Volta’s pile (1800), explain how it illustrates source of potential difference.
items.answer: Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cloth soaked in salt water, making the first battery that produced a steady current. The volt is named after him, and his battery made the study of electric currents possible.
items.markingKey: Context (Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by cloth soaked in salt water, making the first battery that produced a steady current.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The volt is named after him, and his battery made the study of electric currents possible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to source of potential difference.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the length of a constantan wire affects its resistance. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): the wire can get hot – keep currents low and do not touch it while current flows. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. the wire can get hot – keep currents low and do not touch it while current flows); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Learning circuits with simulation software is as good as building real circuits." Discuss.
items.answer: Simulations are useful for understanding, but students also need hands-on practice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: safe, quick, no broken components; shows current and pd values clearly. Arguments against: no practice handling real equipment or finding loose connections; real components behave less ideally. Supported judgement: Simulations are useful for understanding, but students also need hands-on practice. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: A family uses a 2.5 kW kettle for 30 minutes a day, a 0.1 kW TV for 5 hours a day and a 9 W LED lamp for 6 hours a day. Calculate the total energy in kWh per day and the weekly cost at 30p per kWh, and suggest which change would save the most.
items.answer: Kettle 2.5 × 0.5 = 1.25 kWh; TV 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 kWh; lamp 0.009 × 6 = 0.054 kWh; total ≈ 1.80 kWh/day; week ≈ 12.6 kWh; cost ≈ £3.79. Biggest saving: boil only the water needed (kettle is largest use).
items.markingKey: Kettle 2.5 × 0.5 = 1.25 kWh; TV 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 kWh; lamp 0.009 × 6 = 0.054 kWh; total ≈ 1.80 kWh/day; week ≈ 12.6 kWh; cost ≈ £3.79. Biggest saving: boil only the water needed (kettle is largest use).

items.stem: Plan an investigation into how the number of turns on an electromagnet affects its strength, and explain the expected results.
items.answer: Wind 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 turns of insulated wire round the same iron nail; connect to a low-voltage supply with an ammeter and keep the current constant (variable resistor); count paper clips picked up (or measure force on a newton meter); repeat three times; switch off between trials (wire heats). Expect more turns → more clips, because each turn adds to the magnetic field.
